headings.title: Introduction to Cardiac Pacemakers and Indications for Insertion
headings.content: A cardiac pacemaker is an electronic medical device designed to deliver electrical impulses to the myocardium, effectively stimulating the heart muscle to contract when the body's natural pacemaker fails to maintain a normal rhythm. In clinical practice across Nigeria, nursing students must understand that the primary indication for permanent pacemaker insertion is symptomatic bradyarrhythmias. These conditions include sick sinus syndrome, third-degree atrioventricular (AV) block, symptomatic second-degree AV block, and chronic bifascicular or trifascicular block. When the heart rate drops too low, cardiac output decreases significantly, leading to clinical manifestations such as profound fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, syncope, and heart failure exacerbations. Temporary pacemakers may also be utilized in emergency settings, such as during acute myocardial infarction complicated by severe bradycardia or complete heart block, prior to permanent device placement. As future nurses, recognizing these clinical indications allows for prompt identification of patients requiring intervention and ensures timely preparation for procedural management. The goal of pacemaker therapy is to restore an adequate heart rate, maintain synchronized atrioventricular contraction, improve systemic perfusion, and enhance the overall quality of life for the patient.

headings.title: Types of Pacemakers and Basic Functioning Modes
headings.content: Pacemakers are categorized based on their complexity, placement, and pacing capabilities into temporary and permanent devices, as well as single-chamber, dual-chamber, and biventricular systems. A single-chamber pacemaker utilizes one lead placed in either the right atrium or the right ventricle. A dual-chamber pacemaker uses two leads, positioning one in the right atrium and one in the right ventricle, which allows for sequential pacing that mimics normal physiological heart rhythm by maintaining atrioventricular synchrony. Biventricular pacemakers, also known as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) devices, utilize three leads to pace both ventricles and the right atrium simultaneously, improving pumping efficiency in patients with severe heart failure. Basic functioning modes are typically described using a standardized three-to-five-letter code established by the North American Society of Pacing and Electrophysiology (NASPE) and British Pacing and Electrophysiology Group (BPEG). The first letter denotes the chamber paced (A for atrium, V for ventricle, D for dual), the second letter indicates the chamber sensed, and the third letter signifies the response to sensing (such as 'I' for inhibited or 'T' for triggered). Understanding these modes helps nursing students interpret patient records, anticipate clinical needs, and monitor device functionality accurately.

headings.title: Pre-Procedural Nursing Assessment and Patient Preparation
headings.content: Comprehensive pre-procedural nursing assessment and preparation are critical to ensure patient safety and minimize complications during and after pacemaker insertion. The nurse must conduct a thorough baseline physical assessment, focusing particularly on cardiovascular status, vital signs, and cardiopulmonary sounds. Reviewing the patient's medication history is essential, with specific attention paid to anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs, which may need to be withheld or adjusted prior to the procedure to prevent excessive bleeding or hematoma formation at the insertion site. Baseline laboratory investigations, including a complete blood count, coagulation profile, and serum electrolytes, must be checked and documented. The nurse is responsible for obtaining informed consent, ensuring the patient understands the procedure, risks, and post-procedural expectations. Skin preparation involves clipping, rather than shaving, the hair in the operative area to minimize skin abrasions and subsequent risk of infection. The nurse must also ensure the patient fasts as ordered, usually from midnight or for at least six hours prior to the procedure. Finally, establishing secure intravenous access and administering any ordered preoperative prophylactic antibiotics complete the vital preparatory steps.

headings.title: Immediate Post-Procedural Care and Monitoring
headings.content: Immediate post-procedural care focuses on stabilizing the patient, monitoring for acute complications, and ensuring proper device function. Following pacemaker implantation, the nurse should immediately obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) to verify capture, sensing, and overall device function. Continuous cardiac monitoring is mandatory during the initial recovery period to detect any arrhythmias or loss of capture. Vital signs must be monitored frequently—typically every 15 minutes for the first hour, then every 30 minutes for two hours, and then hourly until stable. The nurse must closely inspect the surgical incision site for signs of bleeding, swelling, hematoma formation, and crepitus. Another critical and potentially life-threatening complication to monitor for is pneumothorax, especially if a subclavian approach was used; nurses should assess for diminished breath sounds, respiratory distress, and chest pain. Pain management is provided as ordered to ensure patient comfort. Additionally, bed rest or restricted mobility of the affected upper extremity is typically prescribed for several hours to prevent lead dislodgement while the surgical site begins to heal.

headings.title: Wound Care and Activity Restrictions
headings.content: Proper wound care and adherence to activity restrictions are vital during the healing phase to prevent surgical site infections and lead displacement. The nurse must instruct the patient to keep the incision site clean, dry, and covered with the initial sterile dressing for the specified timeframe, usually 48 hours, after which dressing changes may be performed using aseptic technique. Patients must be taught to inspect the wound daily for signs of infection, such as increasing redness, warmth, purulent drainage, or fever. Regarding activity restrictions, the patient must limit the movement of the arm on the operative side. For the first few weeks, the arm should not be raised above shoulder level, and heavy lifting (usually anything over 5 kilograms) must be strictly avoided to prevent pulling on the newly implanted leads, which could cause dislodgement. Vigorous shoulder exercises or sports should be postponed until the physician gives clearance following a follow-up check. Wearing loose clothing that does not rub against the incision site can also enhance comfort and reduce irritation.

headings.title: Troubleshooting Common Pacemaker Malfunctions
headings.content: Troubleshooting pacemaker malfunctions requires a systematic understanding of common device issues, including failure to capture, failure to sense, and failure to output. Failure to capture occurs when the pacemaker delivers an electrical stimulus, but the myocardium fails to depolarize, indicated on the ECG by pacing spikes not followed by P waves or QRS complexes. This can be caused by lead displacement, battery depletion, or increased fibrosis at the lead tip. Failure to sense (undersensing) happens when the pacemaker fails to recognize the heart's intrinsic electrical activity, firing inappropriately during the refractory period, which can induce dangerous arrhythmias like ventricular fibrillation. Conversely, oversensing occurs when the pacemaker mistakes non-cardiac electrical signals, such as skeletal muscle activity, for intrinsic heartbeats, resulting in inappropriate inhibition of pacing. Failure to output involves a total absence of pacing artifacts on the ECG, usually stemming from battery failure, lead fracture, or loose connections. Nursing responsibilities include continuous monitoring of the patient's hemodynamic status, recognizing these ECG abnormalities, administering emergency interventions if the patient becomes unstable, and immediately notifying the cardiologist or electrophysiologist.

headings.title: Patient Education on Electromagnetic Interference and Device Safety
headings.content: Patient education regarding electromagnetic interference (EMI) and device safety is a crucial component of nursing care for individuals with pacemakers. Modern pacemakers are designed with protective shielding, but strong electromagnetic fields can still temporarily disrupt device function, causing inhibition, reprogramming, or inappropriate pacing. Nurses must teach patients to avoid or exercise caution around powerful magnetic sources, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines, industrial arc welders, and high-tension electrical generators. While household appliances like microwaves, televisions, and electric shavers are generally safe when maintained in good working order, cellular phones should be kept at least 15 centimeters away from the pacemaker generator site, ideally held against the ear opposite the device. Patients should also be instructed regarding airport security screening; they should inform security personnel about their pacemaker, show their device identification card, and request a manual pat-down rather than passing through full-body metal detectors or security wands directly over the generator site, which can affect programming.

headings.title: Long-Term Follow-Up, Interrogation, and Psychosocial Support
headings.content: Long-term follow-up care is essential for monitoring battery life, assessing lead integrity, and ensuring optimal programming of the pacemaker. Patients require regular device interrogations, which can be performed in-clinic or remotely via telemonitoring systems that transmit data over cellular or internet networks. These interrogations assess battery longevity, pacing thresholds, lead impedance, and any recorded arrhythmic events. Nurses play a vital role in educating patients about scheduled follow-ups and teaching them how to use remote monitoring equipment if applicable. Furthermore, nurses must address the psychological and psychosocial needs of patients living with a chronic cardiac device. Many patients experience anxiety, depression, fear of device failure, or body image disturbances related to the subcutaneous chest lump. Providing empathetic support, encouraging support groups, and offering clear, reassuring communication help alleviate fears and promote effective coping, empowering patients to resume normal, active lives.
